original_question: For n >= 5, let L(sigma) be the odd inversion number of a permutation sigma in S_n, and let L_n(x) = sum_{sigma in S_n} x^{L(sigma)}. Is the polynomial L_n(x) always symmetric and unimodal?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Conjecture 2.2: for each positive integer n >= 5, if L(sigma) is the odd inversion number defined by counting inversion pairs (i,j) with i < j, sigma(i) > sigma(j), and i not congruent to j mod 2, and if L_n(x) = sum_{sigma in S_n} x^{L(sigma)}, then L_n(x) is symmetric and unimodal. citeturn14view0
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's intended target very closely: it uses the same range n >= 5, the same permutation statistic L(sigma), the same generating polynomial L_n(x), and the same symmetry/unimodality question that appears in Conjecture 2.2. citeturn14view0
missing_details: The exact definition of the odd inversion number should be made explicit: L(sigma) counts pairs (i,j) in [n]^2 with i < j, sigma(i) > sigma(j), and i and j of opposite parity. Without this formula, the question is not fully stand-alone. citeturn14view0
It helps to say explicitly that S_n is the symmetric group on [n] = {1, ..., n}; the paper uses this notation in the definition of L(sigma). citeturn14view0

The meanings of symmetric and unimodal should be stated as properties of the coefficient sequence of the polynomial, since Section 2 defines those notions before stating the conjecture. citeturn14view0
The quantifier should be phrased as 'for every positive integer n >= 5' rather than 'always', matching the paper's formulation 'Let n in P, n >= 5.' citeturn14view0

For full self-containment, one can specify that x is an indeterminate and L_n(x) is a polynomial in Z[x] obtained from a finite sum over S_n; this is implicit from the paper's displayed definition. citeturn14view0

The paper immediately notes that symmetry is already explained by the identity L(sigma w_0) = L(w_0) - L(sigma), so the genuinely open content is the unimodality part; that context is absent from the draft. citeturn14view0
refined_question: For every integer n >= 5, let S_n be the symmetric group on [n] = {1, ..., n}. For sigma in S_n, define its odd inversion number by L(sigma) := |{(i,j) in [n]^2 : i < j, sigma(i) > sigma(j), and i not congruent to j mod 2}|, and set L_n(x) := sum_{sigma in S_n} x^{L(sigma)} in Z[x]. Is the coefficient sequence of L_n(x) symmetric and unimodal for every n >= 5? citeturn14view0
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, since the paper observes that L(sigma w_0) = L(w_0) - L(sigma) for all sigma in S_n, where w_0 = n(n-1)...21, symmetry is automatic; so the open content is: is L_n(x) unimodal for every n >= 5? citeturn14view0
justification: This draft clearly targets Section 2 rather than the Coxeter-group problems in Section 1, because the paper first defines the odd inversion statistic L(sigma), then defines L_n(x), and then states exactly the conjecture that L_n(x) is symmetric and unimodal for n >= 5. The nearby context at the start of Section 2 supplies the paper's definitions of symmetric and unimodal for coefficient sequences, which are needed to make the question fully stand-alone. The sentence immediately after Conjecture 2.2 also shows that symmetry is already known from the w_0 involution, so the sharpest alternate formulation isolates unimodality alone. citeturn14view0
